issues.description: The test for 'invalid POST' relies on a lie in the Content-Length header rather than testing a real failure mode.
issues.detail: The test sends body='' with Content-Length: '1' to force a 400. That complects 'empty body' (the real bug class) with 'header mismatch with body length' (a transport-layer fiction the test framework permits). What is actually being asserted about the example's behavior? If the goal is 'empty body raises HTTPBadRequest', send an empty body honestly and assert. The current test's value semantics are unclear.

issues.description: Changing req.stream.read() to req.bounded_stream.read() is a semantic change smuggled in as a test-enabling tweak.
issues.detail: stream and bounded_stream are different identities with different time/IO semantics — bounded_stream respects Content-Length, stream does not. The PR description frames this as 'add req.content_length to req.stream.read()' but the diff swaps the stream object entirely. That is a behavior change to the example, motivated by making a contrived test pass. Name it or revert it.

issues.description: FAQ example complects request validation, stream reading, and status selection in one on_post method to illustrate a header trick.
issues.detail: The PostTest class entangles three concerns — checking content_length, reading the stream, and deciding the response code — to demonstrate one thing: overriding a header in a test. The reader has to disentangle the example to find the lesson. A two-line snippet showing headers=[...] passed to simulate_post would teach the actual point without the resource scaffolding.

issues.description: README diff bundles unrelated stylistic refactors with the documented change.
issues.detail: The PR title and description are about POST tests for things_advanced. The README diff reshuffles imports, rewrites string formatting, swaps str(result.status_code) for falcon.code_to_http_status, and reorders handle() arguments. These may all be improvements, but they are a separate concern complected into one PR, making the actual change hard to review and bisect.

issues.description: FAQ test snippet uses assert((x == y)) and a tuple-with-trailing-comma idiom that obscures intent.
issues.detail: headers = [('Content-Length', '1'),] and assert(result.status == falcon.HTTP_400) are 'easy' shapes — familiar to the author — but not simple to a reader scanning for the lesson. A dict {'Content-Length': '1'} and a bare assert statement would carry the same data with less ceremony. Small thing; the FAQ is teaching material and shape matters.

issues.description: test_things_advanced is accreting independent scenarios into one function with positional resp1/resp2/resp3/resp4 names.
issues.detail: Each resp is a different fact about the example's behavior under a different input. Bundling them into one test function with numbered names complects four independent assertions into one identity ('the things_advanced test') with one failure mode. Separate test functions would make each value's claim about the world explicit and independently runnable.

review.summary: The PR's stated goal — test POST behavior for things_advanced — is reasonable, but the execution complects three separable concerns: a real behavior change to the example (stream to bounded_stream), a contrived test that exercises header-body mismatch rather than empty-body handling, and a sweeping README restyle that has nothing to do with POST tests. The FAQ addition teaches header overriding by way of a small resource class that itself entangles content-length checks, stream reads, and status selection, when a two-line snippet would carry the lesson. Decompose: ship the example change as its own PR with its own reasoning, send the empty-body test by sending an empty body, and keep the README restyle separate. The question that should have been asked first: what fact about the example's behavior are we trying to pin down, and what is the smallest input that pins it?
